question: Is multicomponent CBT-I the recommended treatment for chronic insomnia in adults?
keyResult: Strong recommendation for multicomponent CBT-I; conditional recommendations for multicomponent brief therapies, stimulus control alone, sleep restriction alone and relaxation therapy alone; conditional recommendation against sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy. Based on GRADE review of 124 included studies (89 analysed) in the companion review (PMID 33164741).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

notes: Clinical population (diagnosed chronic insomnia). AASM task force; GRADE methodology.

question: Should CBT-I be first-line for chronic insomnia?
keyResult: ACP recommends that all adult patients receive CBT-I as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence); medication added via shared decision-making only if CBT-I alone was unsuccessful (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).

citation.authors: Qaseem A, Kansagara D, Forciea MA, et al.
citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians.

notes: Not free per OpenAlex. Evidence base: RCTs 2004-Sept 2015.

question: Does the 2023 European guideline recommend CBT-I, including digital CBT-I?
population: adults of any age with chronic insomnia, including with comorbidities
keyResult: CBT-I recommended as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (including patients with comorbidities), either in-person or digitally (grade A). Pharmacological treatment can be offered when CBT-I is not sufficiently effective (A).

citation.authors: Riemann D, Espie CA, Altena E, et al.
citation.title: The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023.

notes: Open access per OpenAlex. European Sleep Research Society guideline.

question: How much does face-to-face CBT-I improve sleep diary measures?
population: adults with chronic insomnia without comorbidity
keyResult: 20 RCTs (1162 participants). Post-treatment: sleep onset latency improved by 19.03 (95% CI 14.12 to 23.93) minutes, WASO by 26.00 (15.48 to 36.52) minutes, total sleep time by 7.61 (-0.51 to 15.74) minutes, sleep efficiency by 9.91% (8.09% to 11.73%). No adverse outcomes reported.

citation.authors: Trauer JM, Qian MY, Doyle JS, et al.
citation.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

notes: Excluded comorbid insomnia. Note TST gain was small and not significant: CBT-I mainly shortens time awake rather than lengthening sleep.

question: Does digital CBT-I work?
keyResult: 33 RCTs; 4719 dCBT-I vs 4645 control. ISI mean difference -5.00 (95% CI -5.68 to -4.33) post-intervention; -3.99 (-4.82 to -3.16) short-term follow-up; -3.48 (-4.21 to -2.76) at 1 year. Face-to-face CBT-I produced greater improvement than dCBT-I (3.07, 95% CI 1.18 to 4.95), within a 4-point non-inferiority margin.

citation.authors: Soh HL, Ho RC, Ho CS, et al.
citation.title: Efficacy of digital cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

notes: High heterogeneity (I2 = 79%). Not free per OpenAlex.

question: Does digital CBT-I improve daytime functioning and well-being, not just sleep?
population: adults with self-reported insomnia symptoms (online sample, 91.1% white, 77.7% female)
keyResult: 1711 participants; dCBT vs sleep hygiene education. Small improvement in functional health (week 24 adjusted difference 1.76, 95% CI 1.22-2.30) and psychological well-being (2.95, 2.13-3.76), large improvement in sleep-related quality of life (-18.72, -22.04 to -15.41). Insomnia improvement mediated 45.5%-84.0% of effects.

citation.authors: Espie CA, Emsley R, Kyle SD, et al.
citation.title: Effect of Digital Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia on Health, Psychological Well-being, and Sleep-Related Quality of Life: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

notes: The program tested (Sleepio) is made by Big Health, which the lead author co-founded; the abstract does not state this, so check the full-text conflict-of-interest statement before relying on it. Self-referred online sample.

question: Do different CBT-I delivery formats differ in remission and adherence?
keyResult: Remission vs control: individual OR = 8.36 (k = 36), group OR = 4.65 (k = 22), fully automated internet OR = 3.87 (k = 50), supported internet OR = 8.35 (k = 19). Completion of all sessions: individual 83.8%, supported internet 70.7%, fully automated internet 58.4%.

citation.authors: Takano Y, Okajima I, Osao M, et al.
citation.title: Remission, treatment response, and treatment adherence across the delivery methods of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

notes: Free copy is a university repository version (OpenAlex). Useful for a line like 'apps work, but people often stop; support helps'.

question: Does self-help CBT-I (books, programs) work?
keyResult: 20 RCTs. Self-help CBT improved sleep, sleep-related cognitions, anxiety and depression. Effect sizes at post-treatment: sleep efficiency 0.80, sleep onset latency 0.66, WASO 0.55. Dropout 14.5% vs 16.7% for therapist-administered CBT. Telephone consultation added benefit.

citation.authors: Ho FY, Chung KF, Yeung WF, et al.
citation.title: Self-help cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

notes: Searches to May 2013.

question: Is sleep hygiene education alone enough for insomnia?
population: adults with poor sleep or insomnia
keyResult: 15 studies; 12 compared sleep hygiene education (SHE) with CBT-I. SHE gave small-to-medium pre-post improvements but was significantly less efficacious than CBT-I (medium to large difference); SHE-CBT-I difference averaged 8% in diary sleep efficiency and two PSQI points.

citation.authors: Chung KF, Lee CT, Yeung WF, et al.
citation.title: Sleep hygiene education as a treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Supports framing: tips alone help a little; for lasting insomnia, CBT-I.

question: Should insomnia medication be started together with CBT-I?
keyResult: AASM suggests CBT-I plus medication over medication alone (conditional, low certainty), and suggests against CBT-I plus medication over CBT-I alone (conditional, low certainty).

citation.authors: Buysse DJ, Arnedt JT, Buenaver L, et al.
citation.title: Combination treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

notes: New 2026 guideline. Reinforces CBT-I as the base treatment.

question: Which CBT-I components matter?
population: adults with chronic insomnia (with and without comorbidities)
keyResult: 241 trials, 31 452 participants. Remission incremental odds ratios: cognitive restructuring 1.68 (95% CI 1.28-2.20), third-wave components 1.49 (1.10-2.03), sleep restriction 1.49 (1.04-2.13), stimulus control 1.43 (1.00-2.05). Sleep hygiene education not essential (1.01, 0.77-1.32). Relaxation potentially counterproductive (0.81, 0.64-1.02). In-person therapist-led best (1.83, 1.19-2.81). Stimulus control associated with better sleep quality, sleep efficiency and sleep latency.

citation.authors: Furukawa Y, Sakata M, Yamamoto R, et al.
citation.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis.

disagreement: Stimulus control (get out of bed) has its own measurable benefit here; no evidence was found that 'stay in bed and breathe' has comparable benefit.
notes: Stimulus control CI touches 1.00, so evidence for it as a separable component is borderline. Authors note possible undetected interactions between components.

question: Is sleep restriction an active ingredient of CBT-I?
keyResult: Sleep restriction iOR for remission 1.49 (95% CI 1.04-2.13); associated with improved subjective sleep quality, sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset.

citation.authors: Furukawa Y, Sakata M, Yamamoto R, et al.
citation.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis.

notes: Same component network meta-analysis as above.

question: Does adding relaxation to CBT-I help?
keyResult: Relaxation procedures were potentially counterproductive as a CBT-I component (iOR 0.81, 95% CI 0.64-1.02); best package was cognitive restructuring + third wave + sleep restriction + stimulus control in-person (NNT 3.0) 'but not relaxation'.

citation.authors: Furukawa Y, Sakata M, Yamamoto R, et al.
citation.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis.

disagreement: AASM 2021 conditionally recommends relaxation therapy as a single-component therapy; this analysis suggests it adds little within CBT-I.
notes: CI crosses 1, so 'counterproductive' is not established. Applies to relaxation inside a CBT-I package for diagnosed insomnia, not to relaxing at bedtime in general.

question: Does stimulus control on its own treat insomnia?
keyResult: AASM suggests that clinicians use stimulus control as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia disorder in adults (CONDITIONAL).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

notes: Abstract does not specify the '20 minutes' detail; NHLBI's insomnia treatment page describes stimulus control as 'getting out of bed if you cannot sleep' without a time.

question: How effective is stimulus control for insomnia?
keyResult: 11 studies, mostly published 1978-1998. Versus passive comparators, stimulus control gave small to large improvements in sleep onset latency and total sleep time (g = 0.38-0.85); versus active comparators, differences were negligible (g = 0.06-0.30).

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Nordenstam L, Alfonsson S, et al.
citation.title: Stimulus control for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Relevant to the NHLBI vs Breus disagreement: getting up works better than nothing, but trials do not show it beats other active approaches.
notes: Old, small trials with methodological uncertainties. 'Similar to active comparators' means it is not clearly better than other behavioural treatments.

question: Do stimulus control and sleep restriction work alone or only combined?
population: older adults (mean age 68.9) with chronic primary insomnia, VA medical center
keyResult: 179 participants: stimulus control, sleep restriction, combined, or wait-list for 6 weeks. No differences between single and multicomponent arms on diary or actigraphy outcomes; all beat wait-list with medium to large diary effect sizes; gains maintained at follow-up. Combined arm had the largest proportion of remitters.

citation.authors: Epstein DR, Sidani S, Bootzin RR, et al.
citation.title: Dismantling multicomponent behavioral treatment for insomnia in older adults: a randomized controlled trial.

notes: Older adults only. Bootzin (originator of stimulus control) is a co-author.

question: Can a stay-in-bed version of stimulus control ('countercontrol') help night waking?
keyResult: 34 participants given countercontrol behavioural therapy (22 immediate, 12 delayed). Countercontrol reduced the sleep complaint for the total group by about 30% at the end of treatment, with gradual improvement continuing through a 4-week follow-up; older people benefited as much as younger.

citation.authors: Davies R, Lacks P, Storandt M, et al.
citation.title: Countercontrol treatment of sleep-maintenance insomnia in relation to age.

disagreement: Closest evidence to a middle ground between NHLBI (get up) and Breus (stay in bed): staying in bed may be acceptable if you stop trying to sleep. Zwart & Lisman 1979 (PMID 429643, DOI 10.1037//0022-006x.47.1.113) compared stimulus control components including countercontrol, but PubMed has no abstract, so its result is not reported here.
notes: Small, old trial; abstract does not define countercontrol. In the literature countercontrol usually means sitting up in bed and doing a non-sleep activity (e.g. reading) instead of leaving the bedroom; it is still an active 'stop trying to sleep' step, not lying still and resting. No comparison with standard stimulus control in this abstract.

question: Is lying in bed awake linked with insomnia?
population: good sleepers (n=150) vs people with insomnia (n=173), China
keyResult: Cross-sectional survey. Staying in bed while awake during the night and in the morning differed between good sleepers and people with insomnia (Cohen's d 1.33 and 0.85) and correlated with insomnia severity; bedtime, rising time and total time in bed did not differ (d <0.01, 0.07, 0.07). Authors note staying in bed awake 'could be only signs of insomnia symptoms'.

citation.authors: Birling Y, Li G, Jia M, et al.
citation.title: Is insomnia disorder associated with time in bed extension?

disagreement: Weak evidence against 'stay in bed; resting is nearly as good as sleep'. No study was found that tested whether quiet wakefulness in bed restores people the way sleep does.
notes: Cross-sectional; cannot show that lying awake causes insomnia. Study type is cross-sectional (closest FORMAT category used).

question: Do people actually follow 'get out of bed' instructions?
population: outpatients with primary or comorbid insomnia in group CBT
keyResult: 40 outpatients. Perceiving fewer barriers to stimulus control/sleep restriction (less boredom, annoyance) and less pre-treatment sleepiness were each associated with better adherence; adherence was associated with outcome.

citation.authors: Vincent N, Lewycky S, Finnegan H
citation.title: Barriers to engagement in sleep restriction and stimulus control in chronic insomnia.

notes: Correlational, small. Supports advice that makes the out-of-bed activity calm and pleasant to reduce boredom and annoyance.

question: Can nurses in primary care deliver sleep restriction therapy effectively?
population: adults with insomnia disorder, 35 English general practices
keyResult: 642 participants. At 6 months ISI was 10.9 (SD 5.5) with sleep restriction vs 13.9 (5.2) with sleep hygiene booklet (adjusted mean difference -3.05, 95% CI -3.83 to -2.28; Cohen's d -0.74). Incremental cost per QALY £2076. Eight serious adverse events per group, none judged related to the intervention.

citation.authors: Kyle SD, Siriwardena AN, Espie CA, et al.
citation.title: Clinical and cost-effectiveness of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy for insomnia in primary care (HABIT): a pragmatic, superiority, open-label, randomised controlled trial.

notes: Open label. Funded by NIHR HTA. Espie co-author (Big Health co-founder; check full-text declarations). Supports 'with a clinician's help' wording.

question: Does AASM recommend sleep restriction alone?
keyResult: AASM suggests that clinicians use sleep restriction therapy as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia disorder in adults (CONDITIONAL).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

notes: Clinical population.

newAdvice: If trying hard to fall asleep keeps you awake, stop trying: let sleep come on its own (some therapists even suggest gently aiming to stay awake).
question: Does paradoxical intention (trying to stay awake) help insomnia?
keyResult: 10 trials. Compared with passive comparators, paradoxical intention led to large improvements in key insomnia symptoms and great reductions in sleep-related performance anxiety; relative to active comparators improvements were smaller but still moderate for several outcomes.

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Alfonsson S, Bohman B, et al.
citation.title: Paradoxical intention for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Few trials; authors call for stronger studies. Pre-registered (PROSPERO CRD42019137357).

newAdvice: If trying hard to fall asleep keeps you awake, stop trying: let sleep come on its own (some therapists even suggest gently aiming to stay awake).
question: Why does trying harder to sleep backfire?
keyResult: Proposes the attention-intention-effort pathway: sleep is a relatively automatic process that can be inhibited by focused attention on sleep and by direct attempts to control it.

citation.authors: Espie CA, Broomfield NM, MacMahon KM, et al.
citation.title: The attention-intention-effort pathway in the development of psychophysiologic insomnia: a theoretical review.

notes: Theory, not an outcome study; explains why paradoxical intention, clock-hiding and 'stop trying' advice might work.

newAdvice: If trying hard to fall asleep keeps you awake, stop trying: let sleep come on its own (some therapists even suggest gently aiming to stay awake).
question: Does acceptance and commitment therapy (accepting wakefulness rather than fighting it) help insomnia?
keyResult: ACT vs waitlist/standard control: insomnia severity SMD -0.67 (95% CI -1.08 to -0.25). No significant difference vs CBT-I at post-treatment (SMD 0.21, -0.02 to 0.43) or 6 months (SMD 0.14, -0.15 to 0.42); CBT-I gave higher remission at post-treatment (RR 0.81, 0.67 to 0.98). Authors: CBT-I remains the gold standard.

citation.authors: Barroso D, de Paula Portilho N, Garbacka-Struzik A, et al.
citation.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy for insomnia: an updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

disagreement: Acceptance-based approaches partly support Breus's 'don't fight it' spirit, but they are not evidence that staying in bed specifically is better than getting up.
notes: Third-wave components also had iOR 1.49 in Furukawa 2024.

question: Does AASM recommend relaxation therapy for insomnia?
keyResult: AASM suggests that clinicians use relaxation therapy as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia disorder in adults (CONDITIONAL).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

notes: See Furukawa 2024 for the opposite signal within CBT-I packages.

question: Does progressive muscle relaxation improve sleep quality?
keyResult: 31 RCTs, 2277 patients. PMR improved sleep quality vs control: SMD -1.74 (95% CI -2.14 to -1.34; I2 = 92.1%); PSQI mean difference -3.79 (-4.78 to -2.79). Also reduced anxiety (SMD -1.11) and improved quality of life (SMD 1.32).

citation.authors: Donato KO, Falcão L, Nishizima A, et al.
citation.title: Progressive muscle relaxation technique improves sleep quality and mental health: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

notes: Very high heterogeneity; effect sizes implausibly large, typical of small unblinded trials in patient groups. Mostly not insomnia-diagnosed samples.

question: Does PMR improve sleep quality, and in whom?
keyResult: 14 studies, 957 participants. Hedges g = -1.24 (95% CI -1.71 to -0.77; I2 = 85.5%). Benefit in adults under 55 (g = -1.40) but not significant in adults 55 and older (g = -1.17, 95% CI -2.67 to 0.32). Number of sessions not related to effect (p = 0.2106).

citation.authors: Li K, Chen S, Liu Y, et al.
citation.title: The effects of progressive muscle relaxation on sleep quality in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

notes: High heterogeneity; uncertain in older adults.

question: Does slow breathing before bed improve sleep?
keyResult: Slow breathing (10 breaths/min or fewer) before bedtime: self-reported sleep duration and quality improved (n = 7 studies); objective sleep findings from actigraphy (n = 2) and polysomnography (n = 3) inconclusive. Slow breathing influenced parasympathetic and sympathetic activity (HRV).

citation.authors: Eide EM, Hernes HM, Grønli J
citation.title: Slow breathing techniques before bedtime and the effects on sleep: A systematic review.

notes: Covers slow breathing in general; does not isolate nose breathing, 4-7-8, box or belly breathing. Applies to relaxation-techniques, 4-7-8-breathing, belly-breathing too.

question: Does 5 minutes a day of cyclic sighing reduce stress compared with meditation?
keyResult: Remote RCT of three daily 5-min breathwork exercises (cyclic sighing, box breathing, cyclic hyperventilation with retention) vs mindfulness meditation for 1 month. Breathwork, especially exhale-focused cyclic sighing, produced greater improvement in mood (p < 0.05) and reduction in respiratory rate (p < 0.05) than mindfulness meditation.

citation.authors: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al.
citation.title: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal.

disagreement: Often cited for sleep, but this trial did not measure sleep.
notes: Outcomes were mood, anxiety and physiology, not sleep. Practised during the day. Senior author Huberman AD popularised the technique; check the full-text COI statement.

question: Does box breathing reduce arousal?
keyResult: Box breathing was one of three breathwork arms; the abstract reports the clearest benefit for cyclic sighing, with breathwork overall improving mood and reducing respiratory rate more than mindfulness meditation.

citation.authors: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al.
citation.title: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal.

notes: No sleep outcomes; box-breathing-specific results not given in abstract.

question: Does 4-7-8 breathing change physiology linked with relaxation?
population: healthy young adults 19-25 (n = 43), with and without sleep deprivation
keyResult: After 4-7-8 breathing (six cycles x three sets), both groups had significantly decreased heart rate and systolic blood pressure (p < 0.05); high-frequency HRV increased in the non-sleep-deprived group.

citation.authors: Vierra J, Boonla O, Prasertsri P
citation.title: Effects of sleep deprivation and 4-7-8 breathing control on heart rate variability, blood pressure, blood glucose, and endothelial function in healthy young adults.

notes: Immediate physiological effects only; no sleep outcome; no control breathing condition. No sleep-focused trial of 4-7-8 in a general population was found.

question: Does mindfulness meditation improve sleep quality?
keyResult: 18 trials, 1654 participants. Versus specific active controls (e.g. evidence-based sleep treatments): no effect (ES 0.03, 95% CI -0.43 to 0.49), low strength of evidence. Versus nonspecific active controls: improved sleep quality (ES 0.33, 0.17-0.48) post-intervention and (ES 0.54, 0.24-0.84) at follow-up, moderate strength.

citation.authors: Rusch HL, Rosario M, Levison LM, et al.
citation.title: The effect of mindfulness meditation on sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

notes: Helps sleep more than attention-matched controls, but not more than established sleep treatments.

question: Does a mindfulness course improve sleep in older adults?
population: older adults (mean age 66.3) with moderate sleep disturbance (PSQI > 5)
keyResult: 49 participants; 6-week mindful awareness practices vs sleep hygiene education. PSQI went from 10.2 to 7.4 with mindfulness and 10.2 to 9.1 with sleep hygiene; between-group difference 1.8 (95% CI 0.6-2.9), effect size 0.89. Also improved insomnia symptoms, depression and fatigue.

citation.authors: Black DS, O'Reilly GA, Olmstead R, et al.
citation.title: Mindfulness meditation and improvement in sleep quality and daytime impairment among older adults with sleep disturbances: a randomized clinical trial.

notes: Small; 2-hour weekly group sessions plus homework, not a bedtime recording.

question: Do mindfulness-based interventions help insomnia?
keyResult: 5 RCTs (n = 520). PSQI SMD -1.01 (95% CI -1.28 to -0.75, I2 = 0%) at post-intervention.

citation.authors: Wang YY, Wang F, Zheng W, et al.
citation.title: Mindfulness-Based Interventions for Insomnia: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

notes: Only 5 RCTs; programs, not apps or single recordings. No good review of consumer meditation apps for sleep was found.

question: Does yoga nidra (guided body-scan relaxation) help sleep?
population: mixed: chronic and acute insomnia, hypertension, COVID-19 health workers, athletes
keyResult: 6 RCTs (n = 244). Most reported significant improvements in sleep onset latency, total sleep time and sleep efficiency, including vs CBT-I, progressive muscle relaxation and music-based relaxation comparators. Most studies had moderate to high risk of bias; adverse events poorly reported.

citation.authors: Dutta A, Mooventhan A, Nivethitha L
citation.title: Efficacy of Yoga Nidra in Managing Sleep Disorders: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.

notes: Small, heterogeneous. 'Non-sleep deep rest' (NSDR) is a branded variant; PubMed has only small performance studies of NSDR, none on night sleep.

question: Does writing a to-do list at bedtime help you fall asleep faster?
keyResult: 5 minutes of writing before overnight polysomnography. The to-do list group fell asleep significantly faster than the completed-activities group; the more specific the to-do list, the faster they fell asleep.

citation.authors: Scullin MK, Krueger ML, Ballard HK, et al.
citation.title: The effects of bedtime writing on difficulty falling asleep: A polysomnographic study comparing to-do lists and completed activity lists.

notes: Single night, small healthy sample, comparison was another writing task (no no-writing control). The abstract gives no minutes figure, so do not quote one.

question: Does a constructive worry exercise add to behavioural insomnia therapy?
keyResult: Behaviour therapy (sleep restriction + stimulus control) with vs without constructive worry. Adding constructive worry gave a larger decrease in insomnia severity (controlled d = 1.10-1.68) and worry (d = 0.76-1.64); no group differences in total wake time or total sleep time; none remitted.

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Lind M, Sunnhed R
citation.title: Don't worry, be constructive: a randomized controlled feasibility study comparing behaviour therapy singly and combined with constructive worry for insomnia.

notes: Feasibility study, very small. Constructive worry is done early in the evening, not in bed.

question: Does scheduling worry for later (worry postponement) improve sleep?
keyResult: Worry postponement plus 'if-then' planning reduced worry duration by about 15 min vs postponement alone, but no intervention arm significantly improved sleep onset latency, awakenings or sleep quality vs controls.

citation.authors: McCarrick D, Prestwich A, Ferguson E, et al.
citation.title: Effects of worry postponement on daily worry and sleep: a randomised controlled trial.

notes: Non-clinical sample. Less worry did not translate to better sleep in 2 weeks.

question: Does a specific imagery task at bedtime reduce pre-sleep thoughts and sleep latency?
population: adults with insomnia (n = 41), single experimental night
keyResult: Imagery distraction instructions were associated with shorter sleep onset latency and less frequent, less distressing pre-sleep cognitive activity than no instructions; general distraction was not associated with worse outcomes than no instructions (second prediction not supported).

citation.authors: Harvey AG, Payne S
citation.title: The management of unwanted pre-sleep thoughts in insomnia: distraction with imagery versus general distraction.

notes: Closest peer-reviewed evidence to cognitive shuffling: an engaging, specific imagery task. Beaudoin's serial diverse imagining studies exist only as conference abstracts without PMID/DOI for the results (see .md).

question: What does the research say about steering pre-sleep thinking?
population: adults; good sleepers and people with insomnia
keyResult: Normal transition to sleep is characterised by sensory imagery and deactivation of higher cognitive processes; insomnia pre-sleep thoughts often involve planning or problem-solving. Strategies tested (mental imagery, hypnosis, paradoxical intention, articulatory suppression, suppression, distraction) were beneficial, negligible, or detrimental.

citation.authors: Lemyre A, Belzile F, Landry M, et al.
citation.title: Pre-sleep cognitive activity in adults: A systematic review.

notes: Beaudoin LP (originator of the cognitive shuffle / serial diverse imagining) is a co-author. Gives the rationale for shuffling but no pooled effect.

question: Does watching the clock keep people awake?
population: good and poor sleepers (n = 60); people with primary insomnia (n = 38)
keyResult: Experiment 1: clock monitors reported more pre-sleep worry and longer sleep onset latency than non-monitors, in good and poor sleepers. Experiment 2 (insomnia): clock monitoring was more worry-provoking than monitoring a digit display, lengthened reported sleep onset latency vs baseline, and increased overestimation of sleep onset latency.

citation.authors: Tang NK, Anne Schmidt D, Harvey AG
citation.title: Sleeping with the enemy: clock monitoring in the maintenance of insomnia.

notes: Small experimental studies; still the main direct evidence. Note: getting up after '20 minutes' requires judging time, so stimulus-control advice usually says to estimate rather than watch the clock.

question: Do gratitude exercises improve sleep?
keyResult: 19 RCTs of gratitude interventions; subjective sleep quality improved in 5 of 8 studies that measured it. Most studies showed some risk of bias concerns.

citation.authors: Boggiss AL, Consedine NS, Brenton-Peters JM, et al.
citation.title: A systematic review of gratitude interventions: Effects on physical health and health behaviors.

notes: Free via University of Auckland repository (OpenAlex).

question: Does a 2-week gratitude exercise improve sleep?
keyResult: 2 weeks of gratitude intervention vs active control (everyday events) and no treatment: increases in hedonic well-being, optimism and sleep quality, and decreases in diastolic blood pressure.

citation.authors: Jackowska M, Brown J, Ronaldson A, et al.
citation.title: The impact of a brief gratitude intervention on subjective well-being, biology and sleep.

notes: Women only, small.

question: Is gratitude linked with better sleep, and why?
keyResult: Cross-sectional. Gratitude predicted greater subjective sleep quality and duration and less sleep latency and daytime dysfunction, mediated by more positive and less negative pre-sleep cognitions, independent of Big Five traits.

citation.authors: Wood AM, Joseph S, Lloyd J, et al.
citation.title: Gratitude influences sleep through the mechanism of pre-sleep cognitions.

notes: Cross-sectional; trait gratitude, not a journaling intervention.

question: Is self-compassion linked with better sleep, and can raising it help?
keyResult: Medium correlation between self-compassion and subjective sleep quality, r = 0.303 (95% CI 0.244 to 0.360). In three experimental studies, small increase in self-reported sleep quality vs control, Hedges' g = 0.484 (0.148 to 0.821).

citation.authors: Butz S, Stahlberg D
citation.title: The Relationship between Self-Compassion and Sleep Quality: An Overview of a Seven-Year German Research Program.

notes: Single research group meta-analysing its own studies; small samples, short-term.

question: Is self-compassion related to health behaviours including sleep?
keyResult: Self-compassion associated with physical health (r = .18) and health behaviour (r = .26); among the strongest effects was sleep. Multi-session self-compassion interventions predicted better health and health behaviour; single-session inductions did not.

citation.authors: Phillips WJ, Hine DW
citation.title: Self-compassion, physical health, and health behaviour: a meta-analysis.

notes: Not sleep-specific; mostly correlational. No trial was found testing 'go easy on yourself after a bad night' as a sleep instruction.

question: Is there a standard sleep diary?
population: adults; good sleepers, insomnia, sleep apnea (focus groups)
keyResult: Expert consensus and patient focus groups produced the Consensus Sleep Diary (Core and expanded versions); Core diary written at a third-grade reading level and instructions at a sixth-grade level.

citation.authors: Carney CE, Buysse DJ, Ancoli-Israel S, et al.
citation.title: The consensus sleep diary: standardizing prospective sleep self-monitoring.

notes: Good resource to link: a free, plain-language diary template.

question: Are sleep diaries recommended for assessing insomnia?
keyResult: Recommended diagnostic procedure: clinical interview, sleep questionnaires and diaries (grade A). Actigraphy not recommended for routine evaluation (C).

citation.authors: Riemann D, Espie CA, Altena E, et al.
citation.title: The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023.

notes: Diary as an assessment tool; also used for sleep restriction.

question: Does white or pink noise improve sleep?
keyResult: 19 of 34 studies had positive findings: 6 of 18 white noise (33%), 9 of 11 pink noise (81.9%), 4 of 6 multiaudio (66.7%). No strong evidence to support auditory stimulation; no adverse effects with short-term use.

citation.authors: Capezuti E, Pain K, Alamag E, et al.
citation.title: Systematic review: auditory stimulation and sleep.

notes: Overlaps environment area (mask-noise-with-steady-sound). Many pink-noise studies use closed-loop stimulation timed to deep sleep, not a steady background sound; check before citing for 'steady rain'.

question: Do theta binaural beats improve subclinical insomnia?
keyResult: Double-blind, sham-controlled: 2 weeks of music with or without theta binaural beats, 30 min before sleep. ISI decreased in both groups with no significant difference (4.41 ± 4.32 vs 2.71 ± 4.66, P = 0.656).

citation.authors: Bang YR, Choi HY, Yoon IY
citation.title: Minimal Effects of Binaural Auditory Beats for Subclinical Insomnia: A Randomized Double-Blind Controlled Study.

notes: Best-controlled trial found; small.

question: Does binaural-beat music improve sleep in older adults in care?
population: older adults with poor sleep in a Taiwanese long-term care institution (n = 64)
keyResult: 14 days of music with embedded binaural beats vs the same music alone; the binaural-beat group showed significantly better sleep quality and lower sympathetic activity than controls.

citation.authors: Lin PH, Fu SH, Lee YC, et al.
citation.title: Examining the effects of binaural beat music on sleep quality, heart rate variability, and depression in older people with poor sleep quality in a long-term care institution: A randomized controlled trial.

notes: Single-blind, small, institutional population; listening was daytime.

question: What does recent review evidence say on music and binaural beats in young adults?
keyResult: 10 trials of music, audiovisual stimulation and binaural beats; most showed improvements in at least one domain (anxiety, stress physiology, mood, sleep quality or cognition), SMDs 0.3-0.6; heterogeneity and small samples limit certainty.

citation.authors: Elnazer HY
citation.title: Music and binaural beat interventions for young adults: A systematic review of effects on anxiety, sleep, and cognition.

notes: Mixes music and binaural beats; sleep not separated in abstract.

newAdvice: Listening to calm music for 25 to 60 minutes at bedtime may help you sleep better.
question: Does listening to music at bedtime help insomnia?
population: adults with insomnia symptoms (13 RCTs, 1007 participants)
keyResult: Cochrane: moderate-certainty evidence that music improved PSQI sleep quality vs no treatment/usual care (MD -2.79, 95% CI -3.86 to -1.72; 10 studies, 708 participants). Low-certainty evidence for shorter sleep onset latency, longer total sleep time and better efficiency (subjective); objective measures in 3 studies showed no improvement. No adverse events reported.

citation.authors: Jespersen KV, Pando-Naude V, Koenig J, et al.
citation.title: Listening to music for insomnia in adults.

notes: Daily 25-60 minutes of pre-recorded music. Strongest evidence in the 'sounds' group; better than for nature sounds, ASMR or binaural beats (no good reviews found for nature sounds or ASMR).
